name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,617

clue.text: Business bureau Tory pal ruined

indicators.note: something ruined has been wrecked out of its proper shape, so the letters must be rebuilt in a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A political friend has wrecked an office or agency's affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Business bureau' reads as one phrase, but 'Business' alone is the definition and 'bureau' joins the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A beauty parlour is a commercial salon, one example of a trading establishment or firm.

clue.text: Vessel fitted with a royal navy hooter

indicators.note: a thing fitted with extra parts has them installed inside it, so the outer word takes in the others

blocks.note: a bowl is a dish or vessel
taken as written
standard abbreviation for the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: A ship equipped with a naval horn or siren.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' and 'royal navy' paint a ship with a foghorn, but the vessel is a kitchen bowl and the hooter is a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Owls are nicknamed hooters for their call, and this pale species is a common farmland example.

clue.text: A writer describing small ski resort

indicators.note: to describe can mean to draw a line round, so the outer word encircles the other

blocks.note: taken as written
a pen is a writing instrument
S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: An author writing about a modest little place to go skiing.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'writer' seems to be an author, but it is the instrument, and 'describing' means drawing round rather than writing about.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspen in Colorado is a famous upmarket American winter-sports town in the Rocky Mountains.

clue.text: Performer having time trouble in 'Beat It'?

indicators.note: having means possessing as well, so the first part is followed by what it owns

blocks.note: a turn is a performer's act in a variety show, and by extension the performer
T is the standard abbreviation for time
to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: A singer struggling with the tempo during Michael Jackson's hit song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat It' looks like the song title, and its quotation marks keep that picture alive; read as an order it means go away, and the question mark flags the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are idioms for fleeing: 'beat it' tells someone to leave, and turning tail is running away.

clue.text: High-flyer once seen going with papers for shredding

indicators.note: shredded material is torn to pieces, so these letters are cut up and reassembled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A former high-flying executive is spotted leaving with documents bound for the shredder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High-flyer' suggests a disgraced executive, but it is a bird, and 'once' marks it as gone. The fodder is two separate words joined by 'with'.
explanation.definitionFit: This North American bird once flew in vast flocks but became extinct in 1914, hence a flyer of the past.

clue.text: Price demanded to remove top of fanlight in America

indicators.note: in a down entry the top is the first letter, and removing it cuts that letter away

blocks.note: in American usage a transom is the small window above a door, which Britons call a fanlight

explanation.surface: A builder charging a fee to take the top off an American window.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Price demanded' sounds like an ordinary quote for building work; it is the payment kidnappers want.
explanation.definitionFit: A ransom is the sum extorted from captives' families or owners in exchange for their release.

clue.text: Member of secret fraternity is unusual bloke

blocks.note: odd means strange or unusual
a fellow is a man, a bloke

explanation.surface: A strange chap belongs to a secret society.
explanation.walkthrough: A bloke is British slang for an ordinary man.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oddfellows are a fraternal friendly society with private rituals, so each of its brothers is called by this name.

clue.text: What is left of engineers sat on electric supply?

indicators.note: in a down entry one part sitting on another is placed above it, so it is written first

blocks.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, the British army's engineering corps
the mains is the household electricity supply

explanation.surface: Asking what is left of some soldiers who sat on a live power line.
explanation.walkthrough: The grim surface suggests charred remains; RE stands for the Royal Engineers, and 'sat on' places them above the supply in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Remains are leftovers, the part still present after the rest has gone or been used up.

clue.text: Rubbish taking E? Take acid!

indicators.note: taking here means taking away, so a letter is subtracted

blocks.note: tripe means nonsense or rubbish
the letter itself, which is removed

explanation.surface: Dismissing ecstasy as rubbish and recommending LSD instead.
explanation.walkthrough: E looks like the drug ecstasy, which fits the acid picture, but it is just the letter taken off the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To trip is slang for experiencing the hallucinogenic effects of LSD, a drug also called acid.

clue.text: Show broadcast mid-spring around 1st of April

indicators.note: to broadcast is also to scatter seed widely, so these letters are strewn into a new order
the first of a word is its opening letter only
around means surrounding, so one piece is placed inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written, hyphen ignored
opening letter of the month

explanation.surface: A programme aired in the middle of spring, around April Fools' Day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' reads as television, which suits a show, but it is scattering letters. Rising Damp was a 1970s British TV sitcom about a seedy landlord.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the title of a well-known British comedy series, so a show is an exact category for it.

clue.text: Hat or hood imported from US to UK

definitions.text: hood imported from US to UK

blocks.note: first meaning: a brimmed hat tied under the chin

blocks.clueFragment: hood imported from US to UK
blocks.note: second meaning: the British word for what Americans call a car's hood

explanation.walkthrough: The clue sounds like a fashion import; the second part asks for the British equivalent of the American word for a car's engine cover.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a traditional headgear with ribbons, and in Britain the hinged metal lid over a car engine.

clue.text: Arcane secret I spread around Ohio

indicators.note: spread out means scattered about, so the letters lose their original order
around means surrounding, so the rearranged letters enclose another piece

blocks.note: taken as written
O is a short form for the state of Ohio

explanation.surface: Someone spreading a mysterious secret across an American state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Secret' sits close in meaning to the definition, tempting a synonym, but it is only raw letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe knowledge understood only by a small initiated circle and obscure to outsiders.

clue.text: Conservative with inclination for housework?

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
a leaning is an inclination or tendency

explanation.surface: Asking whether a Tory is keen on domestic chores.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that the definition is a loose noun use: the housework itself rather than a fondness for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Dusting, scrubbing and tidying are the core household chores, so the activity names a large part of domestic work.

clue.text: Spongy dessert knight tucks into after a drop of brandy

indicators.note: a drop is a tiny amount of liquid, so only the opening letter is poured out
to tuck into something is to get inside it, so one piece goes within another
after places one part behind the other in the finished word

blocks.note: taken as written
opening letter of the spirit
a sorbet is a frozen fruit dessert
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A knight eats a spongy pudding after a nip of brandy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spongy dessert' reads as one phrase, a sponge pudding, but 'Spongy' alone is the definition; 'tucks into' looks like eating and means going inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Something absorbent soaks up liquid readily, just as a sponge does.

clue.text: Scottish man in French article

blocks.note: first meaning: a man's name, short for Leslie, a name of Scottish origin
second meaning: the plural form of 'the' in French

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a Scot appearing in a newspaper story; 'article' is the grammatical kind, and the man is just a short first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Leslie began as a Scottish surname and place name, and its short form is a familiar male first name; in French grammar it is the plural definite article.

clue.text: Get used to a convention in conversation

definitions.note: the answer means make used to; 'get' is read as cause someone to become

indicators.note: conversation is spoken, so the words count by their sound rather than their spelling

blocks.note: a custom is a convention or established practice

explanation.surface: Advice on adapting to an etiquette that turns up when people talk.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken quickly, the two words run together into one verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To accustom someone is to make them familiar with something through repetition until it feels normal.

clue.text: Coach player on the bench knocked over

indicators.note: something knocked over ends up the other way round, so the letters run backwards in this across entry

blocks.note: a sub, or substitute, waits on the bench during a match

explanation.surface: A team coach knocks over a reserve player sitting on the bench.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' looks like the team's trainer, which fits the bench and players; it is the vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A coach is a single-decker passenger road vehicle, a long-distance kind of omnibus.

clue.text: Boffin that relations must visit in the country

indicators.note: a visitor goes in to somebody's home, so this piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: a brain is a clever person, as a boffin is
'it' is slang for sex, as are sexual relations

explanation.surface: A scientist whose family insist on calling on him out in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relations' suggests relatives visiting, but it means sexual relations, and a boffin is British slang for a scientist or brainy expert.
explanation.definitionFit: Great Britain is the island nation containing England, Scotland and Wales, often loosely used for the whole state.

clue.text: Low clerk must change to become major US artist

indicators.note: changing something alters its form, so the letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lowly office worker must transform himself into a great American painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low' looks like a description of the clerk's status, but it is part of the raw letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Norman Rockwell was a celebrated twentieth-century American illustrator, famous for his Saturday Evening Post magazine covers.

clue.text: People who laze around in casual footwear

blocks.note: first meaning: idlers who avoid work
second meaning: slip-on leather shoes without laces

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures idlers dressed in comfortable shoes; the two halves are separate meanings of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: To loaf is to idle away time, so idlers are named for it, and lace-free slip-on shoes carry the same name.

clue.text: Look in Iron City for serious American crime

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
lo is an old word meaning look or behold
NY is New York City

explanation.surface: Searching an industrial city for a major American crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iron City' reads as a nickname such as Pittsburgh's, but the two words give separate pieces that close round the look.
explanation.definitionFit: In US law a felony is a grave offence, punishable by more than a year in prison, as opposed to a misdemeanour.

clue.text: Statesman and duke seen with Benjamin Netanyahu?

indicators.note: one thing seen with another appears alongside it, so the parts are placed side by side

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for duke
Netanyahu is an Israeli prime minister

explanation.surface: A politician and an aristocrat photographed beside Israel's prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that Netanyahu stands for his nationality; the shared first name Benjamin is a nod to the answer's own first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Benjamin Disraeli was a Victorian Conservative prime minister of Britain, a leading politician of his age.

clue.text: A French young man going around about naked

indicators.note: going round something brings a traveller to its far side, so this piece is set down after the next one

blocks.note: un is French for a
C stands for circa, Latin for about
a lad is a boy or young man

explanation.surface: A young Frenchman wandering about without clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: Read strictly as a container, the lad round C would give the wrong order; the young man coming round to stand after the C is the reading that fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Unclad is a literary adjective for undressed, describing someone wearing no clothing at all.

clue.text: Country friend you might hear of in Bow

definitions.text: friend you might hear of in Bow

blocks.note: first meaning: the nation in East Asia

blocks.clueFragment: friend you might hear of in Bow
blocks.note: second meaning: Cockney rhyming slang

explanation.walkthrough: Bow is an East London district whose bells define a true Cockney; in Cockney rhyming slang 'china plate' rhymes with mate, shortened to the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the large East Asian republic, and in East London slang a word for a pal or companion.

clue.text: Evil, manly and physically aggressive? Not I!

indicators.note: 'not' tells the solver to go without the letter named, so it is taken out

blocks.note: male means masculine or manly
violent means using physical force

explanation.surface: Someone protesting that they are not a cruel, macho bully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not I!' sounds like a denial; it is an instruction to drop the letter I from the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Malevolent describes someone wishing harm on others, a close synonym for wicked or malicious.

clue.text: Sex with Hoskins repelled couple

indicators.note: something repelled is driven back, so its letters run in the opposite direction

blocks.note: 'it' is slang for sex
Hoskins is the setter, who refers to himself

explanation.surface: A couple repelled by the idea of sex with the setter.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's own name stands for the first person, a common self-deprecating crossword joke.
explanation.definitionFit: An item is informal for two people in a romantic relationship, as in 'they are an item'.

clue.text: Do many bets annoy? No way!

indicators.note: to do something over is to treat it roughly, so the letters are worked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A gambler's partner asks whether all the wagers are irritating, and gets an emphatic denial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' looks like the auxiliary starting a question, but it is the signal to rework the letters that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are emphatic idioms of refusal or denial, meaning certainly not under any circumstances.
